intro: In 1920 the federal government was small enough that most Americans met it only at the post office. By 1973 it ran old-age pensions and hospital insurance, guaranteed home loans and bank deposits, built a forty-thousand-mile highway system, stationed soldiers on four continents, and had put men on the Moon. Between those two dates the country lived through the biggest economic collapse in its history, the largest war ever fought, and a thirty-year standoff with the Soviet Union in which both sides kept enough weapons to end human life. Nearly every argument about government that Americans have today began in those fifty years.

This unit follows that story through people and places you can picture: a line outside a locked bank in a central Illinois town in March 1933; a squash court under the University of Chicago's football stands where the atomic age began in December 1942; a Japanese American family locking their farmhouse for a camp in the desert; a president reading photographs of missiles in Cuba over breakfast; and Michigan Avenue in August 1968, filled with tear gas and television cameras. Where the evidence allows, you will see the same event from more than one side: the worker and the owner, the general and the draftee, the senator and the witness he accused.

By the end you should be able to explain how the Depression and the war remade the federal government, how the Cold War shaped daily life from the suburbs to the schoolroom, and why Americans left this era more powerful, more prosperous and more divided than they had entered it. Most of all you should be able to argue, with dates, numbers and sources, about the question that runs through all three chapters: how much power should a government take in a crisis, and what should it give back when the crisis ends?
bigQuestion: From the Depression through Vietnam, Americans gave their government enormous new powers to fight crises at home and abroad. Did that power protect freedom, threaten it, or both?

timeline.t: Prohibition takes effect and the first commercial radio station goes on the air in Pittsburgh
The stock market crashes, exposing an economy built on debt and speculation
Roosevelt takes office, closes every bank, and the Hundred Days begin
Social Security, the Wagner Act and the WPA create the Second New Deal
Japan attacks Pearl Harbor; the United States enters the Second World War
Fermi's team achieves the first controlled chain reaction under Stagg Field in Chicago
Allied forces land in Normandy on D-Day
Atomic bombs destroy Hiroshima and Nagasaki; Japan surrenders
The Truman Doctrine, the Marshall Plan, the Berlin airlift and NATO set containment in place
The Korean War ends near the line where it began
The Cuban Missile Crisis brings the superpowers to the edge of nuclear war
The Tet Offensive, two assassinations and the Chicago convention shake the country

words.d: paying for a car or radio in small monthly payments with interest, which spread consumer debt in the 1920s
the national ban on making, selling or transporting alcohol under the Eighteenth Amendment, 1920 to 1933
Roosevelt's programs of the 1930s that put the federal government into banking, farming, jobs, labor and old-age insurance
the 1935 system of federal old-age pensions and unemployment insurance paid for by payroll taxes
the drought and dust storms of the 1930s on the southern Plains that drove hundreds of thousands off the land
the 1941 law that let the United States supply weapons to Britain and other Allies before entering the war
Roosevelt's 1942 order that led to the removal and incarceration of about 120,000 Japanese Americans
the secret wartime program that built the atomic bomb, with its first chain reaction achieved in Chicago
the Cold War policy of stopping communism from spreading beyond where it already held power
the accusations, investigations and blacklists of the early 1950s aimed at suspected Communists, often without evidence
Lyndon Johnson's programs of 1964 and 1965, including Medicare, Medicaid, federal school aid and the war on poverty
the surprise Communist attacks across South Vietnam in early 1968 that turned many Americans against the war

test.q: Why did a bank run in March 1933 threaten even a sound bank?
choices: A bank lends out most of its deposits, so it cannot pay every depositor at once if they all demand cash
Banks were forbidden to hold cash
The government had already taken the deposits
Depositors could only withdraw gold
test.why: Banks keep only a small share of deposits as cash; a panic that brings everyone to the window at once empties the vault of even a healthy bank.

test.q: Which best describes the economy of the late 1920s that the crash of October 1929 exposed?
choices: Balanced and debt-free
Dominated by farm exports
Shrinking for most of the decade
Dependent on consumer credit and stock speculation, with farmers and many workers already struggling
test.why: Installment debt, margin buying and weak farm income meant the crash hit an economy with little cushion.

test.q: What was the main purpose of the 1924 immigration law?
choices: To welcome refugees from Europe
To sharply cut immigration from southern and eastern Europe and bar it from Asia through national quotas
To recruit workers for Chicago factories
To end all immigration from Mexico
test.why: The quotas favored northern and western Europe and reflected the nativism that also fed the Klan's revival.

test.q: How did the Second New Deal of 1935 differ from the Hundred Days of 1933?
choices: It created lasting institutions such as Social Security and the right to unionize rather than emergency relief alone
It repealed most of the first New Deal
It focused only on banking
It was passed by Hoover
test.why: The 1933 laws answered the emergency; the 1935 laws built permanent structures that still exist.

test.q: What happened when Roosevelt proposed adding justices to the Supreme Court in 1937?
choices: Congress passed the plan and the Court grew to fifteen
The Court resigned in protest
Roosevelt withdrew the plan before Congress saw it
Congress rejected the plan, but the Court soon began upholding New Deal laws anyway
test.why: The court-packing bill failed, yet the Court shifted and retirements let Roosevelt name new justices.

test.q: What did the Neutrality Acts of the 1930s show about American opinion?
choices: Most Americans wanted to join Britain immediately
Congress favored an alliance with Germany
Most Americans wanted to stay out of another European war after the First World War
The public expected war with Japan
test.why: The laws barred arms sales and loans to nations at war because the public blamed bankers and arms makers for 1917.

test.q: On what grounds did the government remove about 120,000 Japanese Americans from the West Coast in 1942?
choices: Claimed military necessity, though no charges were filed and most of those removed were citizens
Convictions for spying
Their own request for protection
A treaty with Japan
test.why: Executive Order 9066 rested on ancestry, not evidence; the government later admitted no military need had been shown.

test.q: Why did the United States land in Normandy in June 1944 rather than earlier?
choices: Germany had already surrendered in the east
The Soviets asked the Allies to wait
Britain refused to take part
Building the ships, planes and trained forces for a cross-Channel invasion took years, while the Soviets bore the main fighting
test.why: D-Day required enormous preparation; meanwhile the Eastern Front wore the German army down.

test.q: What was the significance of the experiment under Stagg Field on December 2, 1942?
choices: It was the first test of an atomic bomb
It proved a controlled nuclear chain reaction was possible, opening the way to the bomb
It ended the Manhattan Project
It produced electricity for Chicago
test.why: Fermi's pile showed the reaction could be started and stopped; the bomb itself was tested in New Mexico in 1945.

test.q: What did the Truman Doctrine of 1947 commit the United States to do?
choices: Support free peoples resisting takeover by armed minorities or outside pressure, beginning with Greece and Turkey
Invade the Soviet Union
Withdraw from Europe
Share the atomic bomb with allies
test.why: Truman's speech to Congress made containment of communism the declared policy of the United States.

test.q: How did the Korean War end in 1953?
choices: With the unification of Korea under the South
With a Chinese surrender
With a United Nations occupation of the North
With an armistice near the 38th parallel, roughly where the war had begun
test.why: After three years and about thirty-six thousand American deaths, the border returned close to its starting line.

test.q: What finally turned public opinion against Senator McCarthy in 1954?
choices: A Supreme Court ruling
He confessed to inventing his lists
Televised Army hearings that let millions watch his methods, and the Senate's censure that followed
He lost his election
test.why: Seeing McCarthy on television, and Welch's rebuke, cost him support; the Senate censured him in December 1954.

test.q: How was the Cuban Missile Crisis resolved in October 1962?
choices: The Soviets agreed to remove the missiles after a U.S. naval quarantine and a pledge not to invade Cuba, with a private promise about missiles in Turkey
The United States invaded Cuba
Cuba expelled the Soviet troops
The United Nations took control of the missiles
test.why: Kennedy chose a blockade over an air strike, and a public and a secret deal ended the crisis without war.

test.q: Which was a result of Johnson's Great Society programs?
choices: The poverty rate rose sharply
Medicare was repealed
Federal aid to schools was banned
The poverty rate fell from about nineteen percent in 1964 to about twelve percent by 1969
test.why: Medicare, Medicaid, food aid and school aid coincided with a large drop in poverty, though critics argue about how much was due to the economy.

test.q: Why did the 1968 Democratic convention in Chicago hurt the party in that year's election?
choices: The convention nominated no one
Television showed police beating protesters while the party nominated a candidate tied to the war, splitting Democrats and helping Nixon
The convention was moved to Miami
Mayor Daley endorsed Nixon
test.why: The Walker Report called the violence a police riot; the images and the party's division over Vietnam aided Nixon's narrow win.

write.prompt: Make a claim: Between 1933 and 1973, did the growth of federal power do more to protect Americans' freedom or to endanger it? Support your claim with at least three pieces of evidence from the unit, explain your reasoning and answer the strongest evidence against your claim.
tips: State your claim in one sentence, taking a clear side while admitting the strongest exception.
Draw evidence from more than one chapter: a New Deal program, a wartime action such as Executive Order 9066 or the GI Bill, and a Cold War event such as McCarthyism or the draft.
Use specific dates, numbers from the data tables and words from the sources, not general impressions.
Explain how each piece of evidence supports your claim, not just what happened.
State the best case for the other side fairly, then explain why your claim still holds.
